title: Memoirs of Amorous Gentlemen by Leah Nanako Winkler and Duncan Sheik ...
transcript: With the scenic design of Cabaret, the storytelling sensibility of Moulin Rouge, and the rhyming schemes of Dr. Seuss comes a new musical, Memoirs of Amorous Gentlemen. Based on the manga of the same name, it follows a young woman named Colette documenting her experiences as a sex worker at The Night Egg. This sleek production touts a glitzy, immersive design and shining vocals, especially from its central couple, Colette and Leon, but struggles to crystallize its many ideas in a brief hundred minutes or so. Unexpected circumstances turn Colette to writing, and a more assured sense of self and life's meaning comes to her from unexpected people. She, the other women at The Night Egg, and many of their clients live on the fringes of society with far more to offer than they're credited for. Attention has been paid to Colette's character development, but the rest of them come in and out like a revolving door of perspectives, never truly finding enough footing to justify their own songs. That said, the score has the melodic expressiveness that the late, great Duncan Sheik has been known to deliver, with Colette's midshow park-and-bark ballad being the crown jewel of the entire show. Elsewhere, the lyricism is often clunky, dampening the edgy and seductive vibe the show seems to otherwise be going for. While I can stand behind the premise, I think the show is a little misaligned in its current state, prioritizing the visual experience over the storytelling. I wish it had gone through another workshop — it has so much more to say than it has to show for it, much like its protagonist.
